--- title: "Bayesian *t*-Tests and Diagnostics" subtitle: "PSYC 6019-A01 / PSYC 6022-A01
2025-10-13 | Lab 7" author: "Jess Helmer" footer: "[jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026](https://jhelmer3.github.io/PSYC6019-2026/)" format: revealjs: code-link: true slide-number: true code-line-numbers: false theme: ../../gt-theme.scss width: 1200 execute: echo: true dpi: 600 freeze: auto knitr: opts_chunk: dev: svg resources: - ../media/lab_07/samples.mp4 --- ## Outline - *t*-tests as linear models - Bayesian *t*-tests - Diagnostics ::: {.cell} ::: # *t*-Tests as a Linear Model ## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model We can specify a *t*-test as a linear model. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Our goal with *t*-tests is to compare means. $H_0$: $\mu_1 = \mu_2$ aka $\mu_1 - \mu_2 = 0$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} We can estimate the overall mean of the outcome with an intercept-only model, where $\beta_0$ is the intercept. $y = \beta_0 + \epsilon$ Then, we can add a slope term $\beta_1$ to represent the difference in means between groups. $y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \times \text{group} + \epsilon$ ::: :::: ## *t*-Tests as a Linear Model Together, these parameters contain us the same information as a *t*-test. For example, in an experiment, if the control group is coded $\text{group}_\text{control} = 0$ and the treatment group is coded $\text{group}_\text{control} = 1$, ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 =$ mean of control group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_1 =$ difference in means between control group and treatment group ::: ::: subpoint ○ $\beta_0 + \beta_1 =$ mean of treatment group ::: # Bayesian *t*-Tests ## Bayesian Inference So far, we've been working with the frequentist statistical framework, Null Hypothesis Significance Testing (NHST). :::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Frequentist** In NHST, we speak only about *likelihoods*. The probability that we would have observed our data $D$ (or more extreme data) given some null hypothesis parameter $\theta$ E.g., the probability that we would observe a mean difference on a test of $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$ points given the true mean difference in the population is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 0$. $P(D | \theta)$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Bayesian** What we as researchers are often more interested in is the probability that a parameter $\theta$ is the true parameter given data $D$ we have observed. E.g., given that we have observed a mean difference of $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$, what is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 0$? What is the probability that the true mean difference is $\bar{x}_\text{treatment} - \bar{x}_\text{control} = 5$? $P(\theta | D)$ ::: :::: ## Bayesian Inference In order to get $P(\theta | D)$, we need Bayes' Rule. $$ P(\theta | D) = \frac{ P(\theta) P(D | \theta) }{ P(D) } $$ ::: subpoint ○ $P(\theta | D) =$ *posterior* distribution, this is what we want to create! ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(\theta)$ *prior* distribution, information we know about $\theta$ before seeing $D$ ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(D | \theta)$ likelihood, the same as before ::: ::: subpoint ○ $P(D)$ scaling term, brings everything back down to probability scale. Makes Bayes analytic calulations mathematically challenging / impossible! ::: ::: fragment Motivates *sampling* from the posterior distribution, instead of calculating it. ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-2-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-4-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Getting to the Posterior Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)}$. ::: {.absolute left="18%" top="30%" width="880" height="522"} ::: ## Getting to the Posterior How can we sample from posterior distributions? We can use a *probabalistic programming language*. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ![](https://mc-stan.org/docs/img/logo_tm.png) ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} *Stan* is an open-source probabalistic programming language that's widely used to write Bayesian models. It has a well-developed, user-friendly R interface called `rstanarm`, which we will use! ::: subpoint-narrow ○ Means we can start to work with Bayesian models without having to lean the Stan language itself ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package! ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("rstanarm") library(rstanarm) options(mc.cores = parallel::detectCores()) filtered_mpg <- mpg |> filter(when_any(cyl == 4, cyl == 8)) |> mutate(cyl = factor(cyl)) ``` ::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} freq_t_test <- t.test(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg) freq_t_test ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Welch Two Sample t-test data: hwy by cyl t = 17.586, df = 144.65, p-value < 2.2e-16 alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group 4 and group 8 is not equal to 0 95 percent confidence interval: 9.918065 12.429731 sample estimates: mean in group 4 mean in group 8 28.80247 17.62857 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian") summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.5 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.0 -11.2 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3842 cyl8 0.0 1.0 3981 sigma 0.0 1.0 3619 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3947 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1759 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests A very user-friendly interface to Bayesian models with `Stan` is the `rstanarm` R package! :::: {.columns style="font-size:80%"} ::: {.column width="50%"} `summary()` function contains lots of information about the model: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `Estimates`: means, SDs, and quantiles (can specify with `probs`) for each parameter. ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `Fit Diagnostics`: `mean_PPD` mean of the posterior distribution of the outcome. If `mean_PPD` is very different from what you'd expect the mean of the outcome variable to be, may be an indicator of something being wrong. ::: ::: subpoint-narrow ○ `MCMC Diagnostics`: Diagnostics for the Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampler (more on this later). ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian") summary(bayes_t_test, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 5% 50% 95% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.1 28.8 29.5 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.3 -11.2 -10.1 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.6 4.0 4.4 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 5% 50% 95% mean_PPD 23.6 0.5 22.9 23.6 24.4 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 3925 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4078 sigma 0.0 1.0 3987 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3919 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1701 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Bayesian *t*-Tests :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} `\{rstanarm\}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model. The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used. ::: :::: ## Full Model $$ \begin{aligned} \text{highway MPG}_i &= \beta_0 + \beta_1 \text{cylinders}_i + \epsilon_i && \text{likelihood: a linear model} \\ \beta_0 &\sim N(24, 17) && \text{prior for intercept} \\ \beta_1 &\sim N(0, 8.6) && \text{prior for slope} \\ \epsilon &\sim \text{Exponential}(0.15) && \text{prior for residual variance} \end{aligned} $$ ## Visualizing Results The `bayesplot` package provides many helpful functions for plotting results of a Bayesian model. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayesplot") library(bayesplot) ``` ::: ## Visualizing Results ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-20-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayesplot::ppc_violin_grouped( y = filtered_mpg$hwy, yrep = posterior_predict(bayes_t_test, draws = 50), group = filtered_mpg$cyl ) + geom_jitter(data = filtered_mpg, aes(y = hwy, x = cyl), alpha = 0.3, color = "#011f4b", inherit.aes = F) ``` ::: ::: ## Prior Implications :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Given that the distribution of the outcome following just the priors includes negative values for highway MPG, maybe we can afford to narrow them a bit! And maybe we want to be a little more skeptical of large effects, so we can narrow the prior on the slope, too. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-22-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t_test_from_prior_only <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian", refresh = 0, prior_PD = T ) ppc_dens_overlay_grouped( y = filtered_mpg$hwy, yrep = posterior_predict(t_test_from_prior_only, draws = 50), group = filtered_mpg$cyl ) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Changing Priors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Original Model** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column style="font-size:80%" width="50%"} `\{{rstanarm}\}` generally defines priors on the *z*-scale ("specified prior") and then transforms them to the scale of our variables ("adjusted prior") to actually run the model. The "adjusted prior" is what was actually used. We can choose to specify a prior on the *z*-scale (`autoscale = T`) or as-is (default) (example on next slide). ::: :::: ## Changing Priors :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Original Model** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} prior_summary(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Priors for model 'bayes_t_test' ------ Intercept (after predictors centered) Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 24, scale = 17) Coefficients Specified prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 2.5) Adjusted prior: ~ normal(location = 0, scale = 34) Auxiliary (sigma) Specified prior: ~ exponential(rate = 1) Adjusted prior: ~ exponential(rate = 0.15) ------ See help('prior_summary.stanreg') for more details ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T), prior_intercept = normal(24, 15), family = "gaussian" ) summary(bayes_t_test_v2, probs = c(0.05, 0.5, 0.95)) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 5% 50% 95% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.1 28.8 29.5 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.3 -11.2 -10.0 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.6 4.0 4.4 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 5% 50% 95% mean_PPD 23.6 0.4 22.9 23.6 24.4 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 4061 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4029 sigma 0.0 1.0 3856 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3933 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1894 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Prior Implications :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Implications of our new priors. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-28-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=528} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} t_test_from_prior_only_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, family = "gaussian", refresh = 0, prior = normal(0, 1, autoscale = T), prior_intercept = normal(24, 4), prior_PD = T ) ppc_dens_overlay_grouped( y = filtered_mpg$hwy, yrep = posterior_predict(t_test_from_prior_only_v2, draws = 50), group = filtered_mpg$cyl ) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Credible Intervals :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} **Equal Tailed Interval** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} posterior_interval(bayes_t_test) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 5% 95% (Intercept) 28.051405 29.520887 cyl8 -12.280455 -10.117885 sigma 3.649137 4.404204 ``` ::: ::: Can also get ETIs from the `summary()` function, as before. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Highest Density Interval** ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayestestR") bayestestR::hdi(bayes_t_test, component = "all") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Highest Density Interval Parameter | 95% HDI ----------------------------- (Intercept) | [ 27.89, 29.63] cyl8 | [-12.44, -9.88] # Fixed effects (sigma) Parameter | 95% HDI --------------------------- sigma | [ 3.56, 4.46] ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: # Diagnostics ## Diagnostics Our goal in Bayes is to estimate $P(\theta | D) = \frac{P(\theta) P(D | \theta)}{P(D)} = \frac{\text{prior} \times \text{likelihood}}{\text{scaling term}}$. But most of the time, $P(\theta | D)$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models by drawing **samples** from the posterior with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-32-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ## Diagnostics with Bayes But most of the time, $P(\theta | D)$ is too complex to solve analytically. So, we estimate Bayesian models with Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC). [The job of MCMC is to explore and sample from the posterior probability distribution $P(\theta | D)$ for all $\theta$ at a rate proportional to each probability.]{.fragment} [So, after many MCMC samples, we end up with a density distribution of samples with height matching $P(\theta | D)$, and we can use those samples to make inferences about our parameters and outcomes!]{.fragment} ::: {.subpoint .fragment} ○ E.g., we believe there is a 90% chance the difference in highway MPG between four- and eight-cylinder cars is within the interval [-12.28, -10.12]. ::: [But, all this hinges on the MCMC sampler---we have to check it for evidence that it *sampled well*.]{.fragment} ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} [This is called a *trace plot*. It shows the samplers' samples for each iteration it runs. Can you tell if this sampler sampled well?]{.fragment fragment-index=2} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.fragment fragment-index=1} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-33-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} scale_colors <- c("steelblue", "#D98282", "#6BAE9D", "#8C7AAE") x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} What if I told you we ran another, completely separate run, and its samples looked like this? ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-35-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 2, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) + guides(color = guide_none()) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} Or a third? ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-37-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 3, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) + guides(color = guide_none()) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Often, a good first step for checking the sampler is just looking at what it sampled! :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} A fourth? How much confidence do you have in the sampler now? [Looking at traceplots cannot guarantee the sampler is **correctly** sampling from the distribution, but if we run multiple *chains* (separate runs of MCMC, each doing their own thing independently), we can at least check if the sampler is sampling **consistently**.]{.fragment} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-39-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 4, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) + guides(color = guide_none()) ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Looking at the Samples Our example's trace plots! Also from `bayesplot`. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_trace(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-41-1.svg){width=1152} ::: ::: [Good! They look like "fuzzy caterpillars".]{.fragment} ## Trace Rank Plots These are called "trace rank" plots. They're very similar to trace plots, except they *order* the samples in magnitude. Want to see all chains (colors) equally represented across the x-axis. It's mostly personal preference, but these are sometimes easier to see bad chains. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_rank_overlay(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-42-1.svg){width=1152} ::: ::: [What does a bad chain look like?]{.fragment} ## Bad Sampling Example Messing with the algorithm on purpose to make it sample poorly... :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-43-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_example <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, seed = 12345, chains = 4, iter = 1200, warmup = 200 , control = list( max_treedepth = 2 ) ) mcmc_trace(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-45-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=1152} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} mcmc_rank_overlay(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="5%"} [Ick!]{.fragment} ::: :::: ## Rhat Looking at traceplots is great, but it's also helpful to have a numerical measure of how well the chains mixed. Especially when you have lots of parameters, not just three. [Rhat ($\hat{R}$, read "R-hat") is a measure of convergence among different MCMC *chains*.]{.fragment} [The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains.]{.fragment} ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-47-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-48-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-49-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Bad The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-50-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="30%"} Variance between chain means is sooo different from variance within chains! ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-51-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-52-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="30%"} ::: :::: ## Rhat Visualized: Good The main idea of $\hat{R}$ is to compare the variance *between* chains to the variance *within* chains. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="70%"} ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-53-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column .fragment width="30%"} Variance between chain means is very close to variance within chains! ::: :::: ## Rhat In practice, you want to see $\hat{R}$ values less than 1.01. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.0 -11.2 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.4 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 4061 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4029 sigma 0.0 1.0 3856 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3933 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1894 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2)[, "Rhat"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) cyl8 sigma mean_PPD log-posterior 1.0002263 0.9997811 1.0000078 1.0007192 1.0006277 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) In order to closely approximate the posterior ($P(\theta | D)$, the point of this all!), we need to make sure we have a large number of MCMC samples. But one issue: the samples within a chain are **not** independent samples. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-56-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=576} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} x <- bayesplot::example_mcmc_draws(chains = 1, params = 1) bayesplot::mcmc_trace(x) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="66%"} Do you see how they follow each other around? ESS accounts for that *autocorrelation*. No hard and fast rule, but might be concerned if ESS is lower than 200 or lower than 10% of your total samples. ::: :::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) Let's check our ESS values. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="40%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Model Info: function: stan_glm family: gaussian [identity] formula: hwy ~ cyl algorithm: sampling sample: 4000 (posterior sample size) priors: see help('prior_summary') observations: 151 predictors: 2 Estimates: mean sd 10% 50% 90% (Intercept) 28.8 0.4 28.2 28.8 29.4 cyl8 -11.2 0.7 -12.0 -11.2 -10.3 sigma 4.0 0.2 3.7 4.0 4.3 Fit Diagnostics: mean sd 10% 50% 90% mean_PPD 23.6 0.4 23.0 23.6 24.2 The mean_ppd is the sample average posterior predictive distribution of the outcome variable (for details see help('summary.stanreg')). MCMC diagnostics mcse Rhat n_eff (Intercept) 0.0 1.0 4061 cyl8 0.0 1.0 4029 sigma 0.0 1.0 3856 mean_PPD 0.0 1.0 3933 log-posterior 0.0 1.0 1894 For each parameter, mcse is Monte Carlo standard error, n_eff is a crude measure of effective sample size, and Rhat is the potential scale reduction factor on split chains (at convergence Rhat=1). ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="60%"} ::: fragment ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(bayes_t_test_v2)[, "n_eff"] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` (Intercept) cyl8 sigma mean_PPD log-posterior 4061 4029 3856 3933 1894 ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Effective Sample Size (ESS) Bulk and Tail ESS tell you about your effective sample size in the center (bulk) of the distribution and the tails of the distribution. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-60-1.svg){width=480} ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("posterior") posterior::summarise_draws(bayes_t_test_v2, "mean", "sd", "ess_bulk", "ess_tail") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` # A tibble: 3 × 5 variable mean sd ess_bulk ess_tail 1 (Intercept) 28.8 0.446 4003. 2843. 2 cyl8 -11.2 0.668 4001. 2564. 3 sigma 4.01 0.230 3855. 2609. ``` ::: ::: ::: :::: ## Warnings ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_example <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, seed = 12345, iter = 40) ``` ::: :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.panel-tabset} ### Plot ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-63-1.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lab_07_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-63-2.svg){fig-align='center' width=480} ::: ::: ### Code ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bad_example <- stan_glm(hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, seed = 12345, iter = 40, refresh = 0) mcmc_trace(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) mcmc_rank_overlay(bad_example) + scale_color_manual(values = scale_colors) ``` ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **Output** ::: {.cell} ::: ::: :::: ## Warnings [Stan documentation on warnings](https://mc-stan.org/learn-stan/diagnostics-warnings.html) [`{rstanarm}` documentation on troubleshooting`](https://mc-stan.org/rstanarm/articles/rstanarm.html#troubleshooting){preview-link="} Things to try... :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="33%"} **Rhat or ESS too low?** Try increasing the number of samples (`iter`, default is 1000 for each of four chains). ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Divergent transitions?** Increase `adapt_delta` towards 1 (default is `0.95`) ::: ::: {.column width="33%"} **Max treedepth exceeded?** If everything else is good, probably fine. Otherwise, try increasing `max_treedepth` (default is 15). Add to `control` argument (`control = list(max_treedepth = 16)`). ::: :::: ## Bayes Factors Comparing models to each other. Here, an intercept-only model to a slope-and-intercept model. :::: {.columns} ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # install.packages("bayestestR") # install.packages("bridgesampling") bayes_t_test_v0 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ 1, data = filtered_mpg, prior_intercept = normal(24, 15), family = "gaussian", diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", "bayes_t_test_v0.csv") ) bayes_t_test_v2 <- stan_glm( hwy ~ cyl, data = filtered_mpg, prior = normal(0, 1.5, autoscale = T), prior_intercept = normal(24, 15), family = "gaussian", diagnostic_file = here::here("lab", "model-diagnostics", "bayes_t_test_v2.csv") ) bayes_factor <- bayestestR::bayesfactor_models(bayes_t_test_v0, bayes_t_test_v2) ``` ::: ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} bayes_factor ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bayes Factors for Model Comparison Model BF [2] cyl 9.44e+33 * Against Denominator: [1] (Intercept only) * Bayes Factor Type: marginal likelihoods (bridgesampling) ``` ::: ::: We can say the model with the slope term is $9.44\times10^{33}$ (very large!) times as likely as the model without. ::: :::: ## Lab 07 Assignment Due **Friday**, 10/16!

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
